t: Number Of Ways To Reconstruct A Tree — Ancestry Is Written All Over the Degrees
o: Every pair [x, y] encodes "x and y are comparable by ancestry": in any valid tree exactly one of them is an ancestor of the other, and conversely every ancestor–descendant couple must appear in pairs. We only report whether the number of valid rooted trees is 0, exactly 1, or more than 1. In Example 1 (pairs = [[1,2],[2,3]]) only the tree with 2 above both 1 and 3 works — 1 and 3 share no pair, so neither may be an ancestor of the other — giving answer 1. In Example 2 ([[1,2],[2,3],[1,3]]) several trees fit, e.g. chains 1→2→3 and 2→1→3 both reproduce all three pairs, so the capped answer is 2. In Example 3 ([[1,2],[2,3],[2,4],[1,5]]) no node relates to all four others even though a root must be an ancestor of everyone, giving 0. The structural facts that power both solutions: the root has degree n−1 in the pairs-graph, degrees never increase going down the tree, and a node's neighbor set is exactly its ancestors plus descendants.
k: The root must appear in a pair with every other node — degree n−1 in the pairs-graph; no such node means answer 0.
A node's parent is its neighbor with the smallest degree among neighbors of degree ≥ its own, and then adj[u] − {parent} ⊆ adj[parent] must hold.
When a node and its chosen parent share the same degree they are interchangeable — more than one tree exists, so cap the final answer at 2.

a.i: A rooted tree is fully described by its layers: level 0 holds the root, level 1 its children, and so on. Translating the pair condition into layer rules: every node must be adjacent to ALL nodes of every EARLIER layer (they are its ancestors), no two nodes of the same layer may be adjacent (siblings are never ancestor-related), and nothing constrains later layers directly. Enumerate all such partitions depth-first, summing constructions, and cap the count at 2 since only the values 0, 1 and 2 matter. Exponential, but it is the definition-faithful baseline that the greedy method below provably collapses.
s: Build adjacency sets from pairs; let n be the number of distinct nodes.
Find root candidates: nodes adjacent to all other n−1 nodes; return 0 if none exists.
Recursively choose the next layer as any subset of remaining nodes that is pairwise non-adjacent internally, adjacent to every node of all previous layers, and adjacent to every remaining node.
Descend into the leftover nodes with the chosen layer appended to the ancestry; add up completed constructions.
Cap the total at 2 before returning.
a.t: Exponential — roughly O(2^n · n²): every subset of the remaining nodes is tried as the next layer at every step; practical only for a handful of nodes
a.sp: O(n + E) — adjacency sets plus recursion state, where E = pairs.length

a.n: Approach 2: Greedy Parent Selection with Degree Checks
a.i: Degrees in the pairs-graph encode ancestry volume: every ancestor and descendant of u is its neighbor, so a node's parent always has degree ≥ deg(u), with equality exactly when parent and child can swap. Hence each node's parent must be its neighbor of smallest degree among those with degree ≥ deg(u), and — because ancestors relate to everything their descendants relate to — the validation adj[u] − {parent} ⊆ adj[parent] must hold; failing any node proves no tree exists. Whenever deg(u) equals deg(parent) the two positions are interchangeable, producing a second distinct tree. One linear pass over nodes and adjacency entries therefore decides 0/1/2.
s: Build adjacency sets from pairs; n = number of distinct nodes.
Locate the root: a node adjacent to all other n−1 nodes; return 0 if none exists.
For every other node u, pick its parent: the neighbor with the smallest degree that is still ≥ deg(u); return 0 if no such neighbor exists.
Verify every other neighbor of u is also a neighbor of the parent (adj[u] − {parent} ⊆ adj[parent]); otherwise return 0.
If deg(u) == deg(parent), record ambiguity; finish by returning min(recorded answer, 2).
a.t: O(n + E) — each adjacency entry is inspected a constant number of times while choosing parents and validating subsets (E = pairs.length)

w: In an interview, derive the three degree facts aloud, then implement Approach 2 — it is short, near-linear, and every failure mode maps cleanly onto one of the three return values. Pitfalls: forgetting the equal-degree swap rule and returning 1 where 2 is required; validating only degrees without the subset check adj[u] − {parent} ⊆ adj[parent] (equal degrees alone do not certify a tree); treating pairs as ordered (the relation is symmetric ancestry); and mishandling multiple nodes with degree n−1 — several such nodes are mutually adjacent with equal degrees, which correctly resolves to 2. Edge cases: a single pair yields two mirror trees (answer 2); duplicated neighborhoods among mere siblings do NOT create ambiguity because swapping them changes nothing — only a parent–child degree tie does. Follow-ups: output one valid tree explicitly (parent pointers fall out of Approach 2), count the exact number of trees modulo p, or generalize to forests where several roots are allowed.
